items.q: Do I need an account to get a plan?
items.a: No. The survey is open to everyone and you can build a full plan without signing up. An account is only needed if you want to save a plan and come back to it later.

No. SproutFund is an educational tool. It explains common strategies in plain language based on what you tell us, but it does not know your full financial picture and is not a substitute for a licensed financial advisor.

items.q: How much do I need to start?
items.a: One dollar. The plans are organised into three budget tiers starting at $1, because the right first move at $200 is genuinely different from the right first move at $20,000.

items.q: What does it actually ask me?
items.a: Three things: how much you want to invest, when you want to see returns, and how much risk you are comfortable with. It takes about two minutes.

items.q: What if I do not understand the terminology?
items.a: Every recommendation is written in plain language, and the glossary covers 32 common investing terms across 7 topics. Terms used in the survey link straight to their definitions.
No. SproutFund is free to use and does not ask for a credit card.

glossary.label: Learning Center
glossary.title: Investment Glossary
glossary.description: Browse simple definitions for common investing terms used throughout SproutFund.
glossary.empty: No glossary terms found. Try another search.

1.definition: An ETF is a group of investments bundled together that you can buy and sell like a normal stock.

2.definition: Putting your money into different types of investments so you do not lose everything if one performs badly.

3.definition: You earn money not only from your original investment, but also from the money your investment already earned.

4.definition: How much the price of an investment can change over time.

5.definition: A type of investment fund that tracks a market index like the S&P 500.

6.definition: A savings account where you leave your money untouched for a set amount of time in exchange for guaranteed interest.

7.definition: An investment where you lend money to a government or company in exchange for regular interest payments.

8.definition: A very low-risk investment where you lend money to the U.S. government for a short period of time and earn a small profit back.

9.definition: Stocks that regularly pay a portion of company profits to shareholders as dividends.

10.definition: The profit you make when you sell an investment for more money than you originally paid.

11.definition: The total value of a company based on all of its shares combined.

12.definition: Small ownership pieces of a company that investors can buy or sell.

13.definition: All the investments that a person owns.

14.definition: A period when stock prices are generally rising and investors feel confident.

15.definition: A period when stock prices are generally falling and investors are worried.

16.definition: When prices for goods and services increase over time, making money worth less.

17.definition: A sudden and large drop in stock market prices.

18.definition: A period when the economy slows down and businesses and consumers spend less money.

19.definition: Money earned regularly with little daily effort after the initial setup or investment.

20.definition: A savings account that pays higher interest than a normal savings account.

21.definition: Investments where you lend money to a government and receive interest in return.

22.definition: The percentage paid for borrowing money or earned from saving and investing money.

23.definition: The amount of money an investment earns compared to its price.

24.definition: Bonds issued by companies to raise money from investors.

25.definition: Investing the same amount of money regularly over time instead of all at once.

26.definition: A retirement account where investments can grow tax-free over time.

27.definition: A group of 500 large U.S. companies often used to measure the overall stock market.

28.definition: A yearly fee charged by investment funds to manage your money.

29.definition: An investing strategy focused on matching the performance of a market index.

30.definition: A strategy where investors try to profit when a stock’s price goes down.

31.definition: Financial contracts that give investors the right to buy or sell an asset at a specific price.

32.definition: Companies that own or manage real estate and allow investors to invest in property without buying buildings directly.

tips.subtitle: Simple, pre-written guidance for visitors who want to learn before creating an account.
tips.headerImageAlt: Two people reviewing financial charts and cash at a desk

tips.disclaimer: These tips are for educational purposes only and are not personalized financial advice.

budget-fit.title: Start with what you can afford
budget-fit.description: Investing works best when it fits your budget. Begin with an amount you can maintain consistently over time.
details: Choose an amount that does not interfere with rent, bills, food, or emergency savings.
Starting small can make investing feel more manageable while you learn how markets move.
A consistent habit is often easier to maintain than making one large contribution under pressure.

emergency-cushion.title: Build an emergency cushion first
emergency-cushion.description: Before investing extra cash, set aside money for near-term needs so you are less likely to sell investments during a rough week.
details: Keep money for urgent expenses somewhere easy to access before putting extra money into the market.
This can help you avoid selling investments at a bad time just to cover a surprise cost.
Review your cushion whenever your income, rent, or monthly bills change.

match-goal.title: Match each investment to a goal
match-goal.description: Knowing what the money is for can make it easier to choose how much risk and patience each investment needs.
details: Separate short-term goals from long-term goals before deciding where money should go.
Money for near-term plans usually needs more stability than money meant for years from now.
Writing down the goal can make it easier to stay consistent when the market feels noisy.

goal-timeline.title: Give each goal a rough timeline
goal-timeline.description: A timeline helps you decide whether your money needs stability soon or has time to handle market ups and downs.
details: List whether each goal is short-term, medium-term, or long-term.
Shorter timelines usually need more caution because there is less time to recover from losses.
Longer timelines may allow more patience, but they still need regular check-ins.

understand-risk.title: Understand risk before chasing returns
understand-risk.description: Higher potential returns usually come with higher risk. Choose investments that match your comfort level and timeline.
details: Ask how much value you could handle losing temporarily before an investment starts feeling stressful.
Money needed soon usually belongs in lower-risk places than money meant for long-term goals.
Compare possible returns with possible losses instead of focusing only on the upside.

diversify.title: Diversify across more than one idea
diversify.description: Spreading money across different investments can reduce the impact of one holding performing poorly.
details: Avoid putting all your money into one company, trend, or sector.
Funds that hold many investments can be one simple way to spread risk.
Check your mix occasionally so one investment does not quietly become too large a share.

watch-fees.title: Pay attention to fees
watch-fees.description: Small fees can add up over time, so it helps to understand what you are paying before choosing an investment.
details: Compare expense ratios, trading fees, and account fees before committing money.
Lower fees do not guarantee better results, but they can leave more of your return working for you.
Review fees when switching platforms or choosing between similar investment options.

hidden-costs.title: Watch for costs you do not notice right away
hidden-costs.description: Some costs are easy to miss, but they can still affect how much your investment keeps over time.
details: Look for maintenance fees, transfer fees, advisory fees, and fund expenses.
Read fee pages before opening a new account or changing investment platforms.
If two options seem similar, lower ongoing costs can be one useful comparison point.

avoid-timing.title: Avoid trying to perfectly time the market
avoid-timing.description: Markets move up and down. A steady long-term plan is often more reliable than guessing the perfect moment to buy.
details: Waiting for the perfect entry point can keep you from starting at all.
Consider building a habit of investing on a regular schedule when your budget allows.
Focus on whether the investment fits your goals instead of reacting to every market headline.

think-years.title: Think in years, not days
think-years.description: Short-term swings can feel loud, but long-term goals usually benefit from patience and regular review.
details: Decide what the money is for before judging daily price changes.
Short-term drops are common, so frequent checking can make normal movement feel more alarming.
Set a review rhythm, such as monthly or quarterly, instead of reacting every day.

headlines.title: Do not let headlines make every decision
headlines.description: Market news can be useful, but reacting to every headline can pull you away from your long-term plan.
details: Pause before changing your plan because of a single news story or market swing.
Ask whether the news actually changes your goal, timeline, or comfort with risk.
A calm review process can help you avoid emotional buying or selling.

plan-ahead.title: Make a plan before emotions spike
plan-ahead.description: Deciding how you will respond before the market gets stressful can make it easier to stay calm later.
details: Write down what would make you review your plan before a stressful market day happens.
Avoid making big changes immediately after fear, excitement, or pressure takes over.
A planned waiting period can help separate a thoughtful decision from an emotional reaction.
